common.footer: Problem-Solving Teaching · PBL units · Runs in your browser — no logins, no data collected.

udl.lead: Practical ways to open the Problem-Solving Teaching PBL units (Grades 3–8) to every learner, organized by the three principles of the CAST Universal Design for Learning Guidelines (version 3.0). Each unit builds from surface to deep to transfer learning and casts students as stakeholders solving a real problem — already building in many of these supports across all seven languages.
udl.howto: 🧑‍🏫 How to use this page: each of the three principles below lists CAST's design options (with their guideline numbers), then a “In these units” box with concrete moves you can make today. Pair it with the ELPS supports page for emergent bilingual learners and the lesson-plan guide for a ready structure.
udl.eng.apply: In these units: students work a real, ill-structured problem as stakeholders — a problem to reason through, not a test to pass (7.3). Nothing here is high-stakes; students revise their thinking as evidence comes in, so effort is safe (8.2, 9.1). Let students pick their own language with the 🌐 menu and choose their stakeholder role and grouping (7.1). The clear surface → deep → transfer phases and the shared Hunches/Know/Need-to-Know chart make the goal visible and mark each step (8.1, 8.5). Use groups so students reason out loud together (8.3, 8.4), and close with the debrief's metacognition prompts (9.3).
udl.rep.apply: In these units: every page runs in seven languages from the 🌐 menu, so multilingual learners can meet the same idea in their home language and in English (2.3, 1.1). Content is chunked into short activities and clear phases students can revisit any time (1.1, 3.2). Where a unit includes a word bank or glossary, pre-teach it to clarify vocabulary (2.1, 2.2). The deep-phase concept map and source analysis make the “big idea vs. detail” and point-of-view distinctions explicit (3.2). Activate prior knowledge in the surface phase and name where the idea shows up elsewhere to support transfer (3.1, 3.4).
udl.act.apply: In these units: students show what they know in several ways — sorting and mapping ideas, building a claim with evidence, taking a stakeholder role, and presenting a solution brief — so understanding travels through more than one channel (5.1, 4.1). Everything works with mouse, touch, or keyboard and runs in the browser with no login, so it pairs cleanly with a screen reader, zoom, or a district assistive-tech tool (4.2). Sentence stems and the 8-part brief scaffold expression while students build fluency (5.3). Have students narrate their reasoning — which evidence, which option, why — to make thinking visible and monitor their own progress (6.3, 6.4).

elps.lead: How to use the Problem-Solving Teaching PBL units with emergent bilingual students, aligned to the Texas English Language Proficiency Standards across listening, speaking, reading, and writing. PBL is language-rich — students discuss hunches, argue from evidence, and present a solution — so scaffolds matter at every phase.
elps.howto: 🧑‍🏫 How to use this page: the four cards summarize the cross-curricular ELPS student expectations for each domain and pair them with concrete moves for these units. The table then shows what each proficiency level looks like and how the activities scaffold it. Pair this with the UDL supports page and the lesson-plan guide.
elps.accom.p: The ELPS require instruction that is communicated, sequenced, and scaffolded to each student's proficiency level. These units do much of that for you: the 🌐 menu displays the page in the student's home language beside English; content is chunked into short activities and clear surface → deep → transfer phases; sentence stems support speaking and writing; and the work is collaborative and low-stakes, so students take risks with new language safely. Turn on the home language during a first read, then invite an English pass.
elps.dom.read.apply: Try this: preview the unit's theme and any word bank before reading (pre-reading). Point out cognates between the home language and English in the sources. Let students revisit the readings and their notes as often as they need — rereading is a strategy, not a failure.
elps.dom.write.apply: Try this: use the sentence stems and the 8-part solution brief as low-stakes writing frames, so students focus on the idea. After an activity, have students write one or two sentences explaining their claim and the evidence for it, using the target vocabulary and a sentence stem.

guide.eyebrow: PBL Facilitation Guide · Problem-Solving Teaching · Grades 3–8
guide.lead: A ready structure for facilitating a Problem-Based Learning unit — surface, then deep, then the transfer problem — following a standard Texas lesson-plan format. A worked Grade 5 example appears at the end.
guide.ex.name: Grade 5 · A New Life — the Immigration Question, 1914
guide.ex.bigidea: People weigh push and pull factors and real constraints when deciding whether and how to build a new life; those choices shaped U.S. immigration and industrialization.
guide.ex.eq: The year is 1914 — should the Baldoni family be allowed to build a new life here, and how?
guide.ex.obj: Students will take a stakeholder role, gather evidence about early-1900s immigration, and propose and defend a solution to the family's problem, citing sources.
guide.ex.lang: Students explain hunches and defend a recommendation orally or in writing — in English or their home language — using sentence stems and a shared word bank.
guide.ex.vocab: immigrate, emigrate, push factor, pull factor, Ellis Island, quota, tenement, naturalization, stakeholder
guide.h1: Building a Lesson Around a PBL Unit
guide.howto: 🧑‍🏫 How to use this guide: a PBL unit runs across several lessons — surface and deep learning first, then the transfer problem. The sections below mirror a standard lesson plan; each one names what to decide and how the unit's phases fit. Pair it with the UDL and ELPS supports pages for the differentiation section.
guide.s1.p: Record the essentials so the plan is reusable and reviewable: teacher, campus/district, grade level, course/subject, unit, lesson title, date, duration, instructional setting (whole group / small group / centers / lab / online / blended), number of students, and prerequisite skills or prior learning. A PBL unit usually spans 5–8 class periods; plan each lesson as one phase or step within that arc.
guide.s2.p: Name the primary standard the unit targets and pull the exact citation from the standards correlation guide for this suite — including the grade's problem-solving-process TEKS, which the transfer phase enacts. Add the ELPS for your emergent bilingual students (listening, speaking, reading, writing) and a language objective. List any crosswalk standards your campus requires.
guide.s3.p: State the big idea / concept the unit builds toward, the unit's driving question (one or two essential questions), and a short rationale — why this matters and how it connects to the unit or the real world.
guide.s5.p: Pre-teach the two or three terms the problem hinges on. Where the unit includes a word bank or glossary, use it. Provide student-friendly definitions, a visual, and sentence stems for discussion — for example, “The evidence tells me ___, so I think ___.”
guide.s6.p: Technology: one device per student or pair, a modern browser, and the unit link — no login and no data collected. Optional: a projector to read the problem and hold the shared KWHL chart, headphones for read-aloud, and printed handouts for offline groups. List any teacher and student materials your lesson adds around the activity.
guide.s9.intro: A workable arc that places the problem at the center, after students have built and organized the knowledge. Adjust the timing to your block.
guide.p2.b: Read the Meet the Problem narrative aloud and think aloud through the first stakeholder question. Model the shared Hunches → Know → Need-to-Know (KWHL) chart, and answer a question with a question so students plan the inquiry.
guide.p3.h: Groups work the problem as stakeholders
guide.p4.b: Students revisit in a second language, extend to a related problem, or answer a short transfer prompt on their own — where else does this problem-solving process fit?
